title: Boolean Operators (AND, OR, NOT), Wildcards & Nesting

content.quick: Boolean logic allows researchers to control database precision and recall. 'AND' narrows the search by requiring all terms; 'OR' broadens it by accepting any synonym; 'NOT' excludes irrelevant domains; parentheses group operations; and wildcards (*) match multiple word endings. PRISMA 2020 requires full audit logging of search strings.

blocks.explain: Boolean operators are fundamental logical connectives used to command academic databases during systematic literature retrieval.

sentences.text: Boolean operators are fundamental logical connectives used to command academic databases during systematic literature retrieval.
sentences.simple: Boolean operators are basic command words like AND and OR that tell academic search engines exactly what to look for.
sentences.plain: Boolean operators are fundamental logical connectives used to command academic databases during systematic literature retrieval.
sentences.technical: Boolean operators operationalize set-theoretic logic across inverted bibliographic indices to regulate document recall and precision.

sentences.text: Using 'AND' commands the database engine to retrieve only publications containing every specified keyword.
sentences.simple: When you put 'AND' between two words, the search engine only brings back papers that have BOTH words.
sentences.plain: Using 'AND' commands the database engine to retrieve only publications containing every specified keyword.
sentences.technical: Conjunctive 'AND' operations execute set intersections across distinct token arrays, attenuating output volume while amplifying contextual relevance.

visual.title: Set-Theoretic AND Intersection
visual.caption: Only papers falling inside the shared overlap will be returned.

sentences.text: In contrast, 'OR' connects synonymous expressions, ensuring that alternate terminologies in international literature are not overlooked.
sentences.simple: Using 'OR' connects alternative words for the same idea so you do not miss papers written by authors who used different vocabulary.
sentences.plain: In contrast, 'OR' connects synonymous expressions, ensuring that alternate terminologies in international literature are not overlooked.
sentences.technical: Disjunctive 'OR' aggregations execute set unions, maximizing bibliographic recall across heterogenous scholarly nomenclatures.

questions.q: Which Boolean operator should always be placed between different synonyms of the SAME concept?
questions.explanation: Synonyms are alternative ways of expressing the same concept, so you want papers that mention EITHER word: term1 OR term2.

blocks.explain: Parenthetical nesting enforces the correct order of operations, preventing fatal logic collapses across complex multi-concept queries.

sentences.text: Parentheses are mandatory when combining different operators to prevent fatal search logic syntax errors.
sentences.simple: You must put parentheses around OR words, just like in high school mathematics.
sentences.plain: Parentheses are mandatory when combining different operators to prevent fatal search logic syntax errors.
sentences.technical: Parenthetical nesting enforces syntactic operator precedence, ensuring disjunctive synonym clauses resolve prior to conjunctive facet intersections.

visual.title: Parenthetical Nesting Syntax

data.meaning: Grouping synonymous terms so the database evaluates them as a single conceptual cluster before intersecting with other criteria.
data.example: Correct: (teacher OR educator) AND burnout | Incorrect: teacher OR educator AND burnout

visual.caption: Without parentheses, the database interprets 'teacher' as a standalone query alongside 'educator AND burnout'.

sentences.text: In the facet building approach, each conceptual column of your research question is enclosed in its own set of parentheses.
sentences.simple: Think of your research as separate building blocks: put all words for Idea 1 in brackets, connect with AND, then put all words for Idea 2 in brackets.
sentences.plain: In the facet building approach, each conceptual column of your research question is enclosed in its own set of parentheses.
sentences.technical: The facet-building architecture groups domain-specific synonym arrays into discrete parenthetical modules conjoined via conjunctive bridges.

visual.title: The Facet Building Search Architecture
visual.caption: Construct your master query block-by-block using this multi-facet strategy.

sentences.text: Failing to nest OR statements causes the database to retrieve tens of thousands of irrelevant papers containing only one of the standalone terms.
sentences.simple: If you forget parentheses, the search engine gets confused and dumps thousands of useless papers on your screen.
sentences.plain: Failing to nest OR statements causes the database to retrieve tens of thousands of irrelevant papers containing only one of the standalone terms.
sentences.technical: Syntax omission eliminates operator precedence boundaries, inducing catastrophic recall inflation and polluting the bibliographic extraction sample.

questions.q: Why will the query 'nurse OR doctor AND stress' return millions of irrelevant papers about nursing history?
options: Because without parentheses, the database treats 'nurse' as an independent standalone search that brings back every paper mentioning nurses
Because academic databases do not support the word 'nurse'
Because 'stress' is not indexed in Scopus
Because Boolean operators must always be written in lowercase
questions.explanation: Databases evaluate AND before OR unless parentheses are present. The query becomes: [all papers about nurse] OR [papers about doctor AND stress].

blocks.explain: Master truncation symbols, wildcards, and phrase quotation marks to capture spelling variations without inflating search noise.

sentences.text: The asterisk (*) acts as a truncation wildcard, retrieving every grammatical variation sharing a common root word.
sentences.simple: Putting an asterisk at the end of a word root (like lead*) finds leader, leaders, and leadership automatically.
sentences.plain: The asterisk (*) acts as a truncation wildcard, retrieving every grammatical variation sharing a common root word.
sentences.technical: Right-hand truncation using the asterisk wildcard executes stem-expansion across tokenized lexicons, capturing morphological derivatives.

visual.title: Root Truncation Mechanics
visual.caption: Truncate carefully: truncating too short (e.g. 'cat*') will match 'catalog', 'caterpillar', and 'catastrophe'.

sentences.text: Enclosing multi-word terms in double quotation marks commands the database to search for the words as an exact, uninterrupted phrase.
sentences.simple: Always put quote marks around multi-word phrases like "job satisfaction" so the words stay together.
sentences.plain: Enclosing multi-word terms in double quotation marks commands the database to search for the words as an exact, uninterrupted phrase.
sentences.technical: Phrase delimitation using double quotation marks forces positional proximity of zero across indexed word vectors.

visual.title: Phrase Quotes vs Loose Words

rows.col2: Words must appear immediately adjacent in order
High (Pulls only literature about the construct)
Mandatory for all multi-word psychological scales

visual.caption: Never search multi-word variables without quotation marks.

sentences.text: Advanced databases like Scopus also support proximity operators such as W/3 or PRE/2 to find terms within a set number of words from each other.
sentences.simple: Advanced databases let you find two words that appear within 3 words of each other using commands like W/3.
sentences.plain: Advanced databases like Scopus also support proximity operators such as W/3 or PRE/2 to find terms within a set number of words from each other.
sentences.technical: Proximity operators (W/n for within n words; PRE/n for precede by n words) operationalize elastic co-occurrence boundaries across full-text corpora.

visual.title: Proximity Operators (Scopus / WoS)

data.meaning: Specifies that two terms must appear within 'n' words of each other in any order.
data.example: Scopus query: teacher* W/3 retention -> finds 'retention of teachers', 'teacher turnover and retention', 'teachers in retention programs'

visual.caption: Proximity operators capture natural phrasing variations that rigid quotation marks miss.

visual.title: Wildcard & Truncation Cheat Sheet
visual.caption: Use exact quotation marks for multi-word constructs to avoid scattering words across pages.

questions.q: What happens if a scholar searches for 'transformational leadership' in Google Scholar WITHOUT quotation marks?
options: The database retrieves papers where 'transformational' appears in the title and 'leadership' appears in the references 20 pages later
Google Scholar automatically converts it into a quoted phrase
The search engine returns zero results
The search query fails with a database syntax error
questions.explanation: Without quotation marks, the search engine treats the words as two independent tokens joined by AND, scattering them across the document.

blocks.explain: Document and log your exact search strings to comply with PRISMA 2020 systematic literature review transparency standards.

sentences.text: International graduate research guidelines mandate that scholars maintain a complete search log detailing every query executed.
sentences.simple: You must keep a written log of the exact search phrases and dates you used so your supervisor can verify your work.
sentences.plain: International graduate research guidelines mandate that scholars maintain a complete search log detailing every query executed.
sentences.technical: Methodological replicability criteria codified in PRISMA 2020 mandate exhaustive logging of bibliographic search strings, parameters, and harvest dates.

sentences.text: Logging exact Boolean strings protects candidates during oral viva examination when examiners ask how the literature sample was bounded.
sentences.simple: Having a clear search table gives you instant proof when examiners ask how you found your papers during your defense.
sentences.plain: Logging exact Boolean strings protects candidates during oral viva examination when examiners ask how the literature sample was bounded.
sentences.technical: Empirical auditability of the bibliographic corpus pre-emptively insulates the candidate against examiner allegations of selection bias or literature cherry-picking.

sentences.simple: Export your search results directly into Zotero so your citations and PDFs are organized and ready to write.

questions.q: Why is it important to record the exact date on which a database search query was executed?
options: Because academic databases add hundreds of new papers every week, meaning the result count changes over time
Because university guidelines expire every 30 days
Because search engines delete your account after 24 hours
Because search strings cannot be run on weekends
questions.explanation: Bibliographic databases are continuously updated. Recording your exact search date establishes a clear empirical snapshot for peer replicability.

mistakes: Searching multi-word constructs without quotation marks, causing words to scatter across unrelated pages.
Omitting parentheses around OR synonym groups, causing syntax precedence collapse.
Over-truncating root words (e.g. 'cat*' or 'pro*') and pulling thousands of irrelevant homonyms.
Failing to record the exact search string, database name, and harvest date in a methodology audit log.
takeaways: Use AND to intersect concepts; use OR to union synonyms; use NOT with extreme caution to filter domains.
Always enclose synonym groups in parentheses: (term1 OR term2) AND (term3 OR term4).
Enclose multi-word constructs in quotation marks: "transformational leadership".
Log your verbatim search strings, databases, and dates to comply with PRISMA 2020 standards.
